newsitem.title: FRANCE: Striking French truckers report progress in talks.
newsitem.headline: Striking French truckers report progress in talks.

text.p: Striking truckers reported progress on Wednesday in marathon negotiations aimed at ending their 10-day-old stranglehold on French roads and the economy but unions and a government minister said differences remained.

Drivers' unions, employers and a government mediator suspended their talks on ending the dispute on Wednesday morning after a 20-hour session and planned to reconvene at 4 p.m. (1500 GMT), negotiators said.
Roger Poletti of the Force Ouvriere union told reporters: "Things have moved forward." But he said some 200 roadblocks around the country would remain in place.

Transport Minister Bernard Pons told reporters after the weekly cabinet meeting he was "neither optimistic nor pessimistic but realistic", saying considerable progress had been made but several points remained in dispute.
Unions said a consensus had been reached on allowing drivers with 25 years' service to retire at 55 instead of 60 on 75 percent of their salary, subject to an overall deal.
But Marc Blondel, FO's general secretary, said employers must agree to pay drivers for loading time and compulsory rest periods on the road if the dispute was to be settled.
The drivers, who have blocked highways, some borders and fuel depots, causing petrol shortages in several regions, are also demanding a 10 percent pay rise and shorter working hours.
It is a key test for Prime Minister Alain Juppe, who is battling to keep down state spending with his approval rating is at an all-time low.
The truckers have mounted around 200 barricades on roads and around refineries and petrol depots across France in a protest that has started to cut deeply into economic activity.
The barricades have forced some petrol stations to close, and petrol rationing has been imposed in some areas so that supplies could be maintained for fire engines and ambulances.
Long queues formed at petrol stations in Bordeaux, the southwestern city where Juppe serves as mayor.
Some factories closed their doors because they could not obtain raw materials while farmers reported spot shortages in animal feed as grain shipments were hit.
The strike was also starting to disrupt mail, grain imports and angering foreign truckers blocked on French roads.

Wednesday was also a test of wider union disaffection in France. The big Communist-led CGT union has urged workers to rally at the blockades to express support and step up pressure on Juppe to drop austerity policies.
But early indications were that there would be few disruptions in other sectors.
Striking rail workers blocked the main railway line from Paris to the port of Le Havre in northwestern France in an unrelated protest over government plans to create a separate railtrack company.

The SNCF state railway company said strikers from three trade unions began blocking the Paris-Rouen-Le Havre line on Tuesday night after calling a 24-hour local stoppage at the depot of Sotteville-les-Rouen, starting point of last year's 24-day national rail strike.

Pilots, stewards and engineers at French airlines also mounted a parallel two-day strike, forcing state airline Air France to cut back on its flight schedule but having little impact on private carriers.
Air France was providing two-thirds of long-haul and just a quarter of medium-haul flights due to the union protest over feared job cuts and restructurings, a spokesman said.
The airline's short-haul unit Air France Europe, which operates mainly domestic routes, was flying fewer than half of its scheduled flights on Monday and Wednesday.
